source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC6137521: the publisher's version deposited by the American Medical Association (JAMA Psychiatry 2018;75(6):585-595; not an author manuscript), read in full on 2026-10-27 in the reader's own browser tab and saved as text: Key Points, Abstract, all sections, the Table (69 rows, parsed and summed), figure legends, article information (funding, disclosures) and the reference list. Step 1 recorded before the card was opened; card check completed 2026-10-30 from the saved text. Figure 1 (flowchart) viewed on PMC's figure page on 2026-10-31, in a new tab of the reader's own, and its printed counts read from the rendered image. Figures 2 and 3 not viewed (every value used for the claims is printed in the text). Online supplement not read.

claims.overstatement: One clause is contradicted by the source's own numbers: the >72 h subgroup's 95% CI is -0.22 to 0.07, so it includes no difference but does NOT include the overall difference of -0.25 (-0.247); the two intervals overlap (-0.22 to -0.17), but the overall point estimate lies just outside the subgroup interval. Suggested wording: 'the interval includes no difference and reaches -0.22, close to the overall -0.25'. Second, '7 of the 15 longer-abstinence studies come from papers by one research group': 7 is the count of rows whose printed reference names Tapert SF; an 8th (Jacobus et al. 2015, ref 62) shares its first two authors with Jacobus et al. 2014 but its printed author list stops at 'et al.', so 'at least 7' is the safe wording. Third, P = .01 is given without 'uncorrected', although the authors describe the abstinence associations as holding 'albeit at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons' (Discussion) and about ten moderators were tested. The claim's overall conclusion (insufficient, disputed) is more cautious than the authors' own conclusion that abstinence beyond 72 h 'diminishes' deficits; given a between-study, cross-sectional comparison this caution is justified, not an understatement.
claims.note: Scott-derived numbers checked: -0.08 (-0.22 to 0.07), 15 studies, n = 928, P = .29; -0.30 (-0.37 to -0.22), 54 studies, n = 7799; chi-square 6.36, P = .01; beta 0.059, P = .04 uncorrected, k = 28 (n = 1661); mean required abstinence 152.7 h (SD 335.2); 22/32/15 studies; 14 monitored: all as printed. 7 to 90 days: confirmed from the Table (168 h to 2160 h). 11 of 15 with age ranges ending at 20 or younger: confirmed (the 4 exceptions: Fried 2005 17-21, Lisdahl & Price 2012 18-28, Murphy 2011 18-30, Price 2015 18-25). The -0.30 (-0.37 to -0.22) value for the 54 studies is printed in the Abstract only (the Results text gives only k, n, chi-square and P; Figure 3 not viewed). Table check: the 15 >72 h rows sum to 410 + 537 = 947 participants, not the 928 printed in the text (and the 54 other rows to 7814, not 7799); the claim correctly uses the text's figure. Two of the 15 'studies' are second rows of papers whose other row is in the <=72 h group (Fried 2005 at 0 h and 2160 h; Schweinsburg 2010 at 48 h and 648 h), so the subgroup contrast is not purely between independent studies, but it is never within the same people before and after stopping, as the claim says.

anchors.extracted: Studies requiring abstinence longer than 72 h: 15 studies, n = 928, d -0.08 (95% CI -0.22 to 0.07), not different from 0; studies with less stringent criteria: 54 studies, n = 7799, d -0.30 (95% CI -0.37 to -0.22); difference P = .01. Overall d -0.25 (-0.32 to -0.17).

At an uncorrected threshold, mean hours of reported abstinence (k = 28; n = 1661) was associated with effect size (beta 0.059; P = .04), longer abstinence going with smaller effects. Required abstinence >72 h (k = 15; n = 928): d -0.08 (95% CI -0.22 to 0.07; P = .29 vs 0), significantly smaller than <=72 h (k = 54; n = 7799); chi-square(1) 6.36, P = .01.
Mean (SD) required abstinence 152.7 (335.2) h; 22 studies (32%) 0 h or unspecified, 32 (46%) 1 to 72 h, 15 (22%) more than 72 h.

anchors.locator: Table (Minimum Required Abstinence Period, h; Age Range; No. of Participants columns) and References 11, 54, 55, 61, 62, 67, 78, 90
anchors.extracted: The 15 rows >72 h require 168 h (7 d: Lisdahl & Price 2012, Murphy 2011, Price 2015) to 2160 h (90 d: Fried 2005 second row); 11 of 15 have age ranges ending at 20 or younger; 7 rows are papers whose printed author list includes Tapert SF (Medina 2007, Hanson 2010, Hanson 2014, Jacobus 2014, Mahmood 2010, Schweinsburg 2010 648-h row, Winward 2014) and Jacobus 2015 (ref 62, list truncated at 'et al.') shares its first two authors with Jacobus 2014; row sums 410 cannabis + 537 comparison = 947 (text: 928). Recomputed mean of required abstinence over the 69 rows 151.8 h (SD 332.5), close to the printed 152.7 (335.2).

Overall d -0.247 (SE 0.038; 95% CI -0.32 to -0.17); between-study variance 0.070 (SE 0.018; P < .001). The >72 h interval (-0.22 to 0.07) therefore does not contain -0.247; the intervals overlap only between -0.22 and -0.17.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Abstinence associations described as holding at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons; only 14 studies reported monitored abstinence; authors suggest residual effects of recent use or withdrawal; findings contrast with a large longitudinal study (ref 102, Meier et al. 2012) and a recent systematic review (ref 25, Ganzer et al. 2016).
Authors note that the National Academies report (ref 91) concluded there is significant uncertainty about cannabis-associated cognitive deficits after sustained abstinence.

No causal conclusions; pre-use deficits not accounted for; longitudinal evidence on trajectories after abstinence described as conflicting (Dunedin decline in a small subgroup versus other longitudinal studies, especially where abstinence was carefully monitored, ref 101).
Only observational cross-sectional studies included; longitudinal studies contributed baseline data only. The abstinence contrast is therefore between studies, not within people.

Authors conclude that abstinence longer than 72 h diminishes cannabis-associated deficits and that earlier studies may have overstated persistence; causal wording stronger than the between-study design allows (the claim is appropriately more cautious).

claims.overstatement: Minor. (1) 'The difference depended on how recently people had used': the moderator is each study's minimum required abstinence (not measured recency), and the authors describe the abstinence associations as holding at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons; 'was smaller in studies that required longer abstinence' would be exact. (2) The statement names visuospatial and motor as showing no clear difference but omits verbal/language (-0.14, 95% CI -0.27 to 0.001, P = .05), also non-significant (it is in the magnitude). (3) 'samples of people seeking treatment differed more' rests on an uncorrected P = .04 (said in the magnitude, not in the statement). (4) 'raw test scores': the authors say their analyses 'primarily' used raw scores; some studies supplied normed scores. None changes the claim's meaning.
claims.note: All Scott numbers in statement and magnitude match the text. Editors' approximate 95% prediction interval recomputed: -0.247 +/- 1.96 x sqrt(0.070 + 0.038^2) = -0.771 to +0.277, i.e. -0.77 to +0.28 (same; with t on 67 df, -0.78 to +0.29). Trim-and-fill reduction recomputed (0.206 - 0.128)/0.206 = 37.9%, as printed. CI from SE: -0.247 +/- 1.96 x 0.038 = -0.32 to -0.17 (same). '69 cross-sectional samples' is a fair label: the paper calls them 69 studies, but several papers contribute two rows to the Table (e.g. Fried 2005, Tait 2011, Schweinsburg 2010). Also noted: subgroup k for treatment-seeking (12) and non-treatment-seeking (56) sums to 68, not 69, while their n (581 + 8146) sums to the full 8727.

anchors.locator: Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph (also Abstract › Results)
anchors.extracted: 69 studies, 8727 participants: 2152 people who used cannabis (mean age 20.6, SD 2.8; 68.1% male in Results, 1472 [68.4%] in the Abstract) and 6575 comparison participants with minimal cannabis use (mean age 20.8, SD 3.4; 55.8% male); published 1973-2017; 384 effect sizes; mean age at first use 15.2 (SD 1.5); 22 studies (32%) required 0 h abstinence or did not specify.
Model without explanatory variables: overall d -0.247 (SE 0.038; 95% CI -0.32 to -0.17); between-study variance 0.070 (SE 0.018; P < .001), more than sampling error alone.

Significant domains: learning -0.33 (-0.42 to -0.24); EF abstraction/shifting -0.30 (-0.40 to -0.20); speed -0.26 (-0.38 to -0.15); delayed memory -0.26 (-0.35 to -0.16); EF inhibition -0.25 (-0.38 to -0.13); EF updating/working memory -0.22 (-0.31 to -0.12); attention -0.21 (-0.31 to -0.12), all P < .001. Non-significant: verbal/language -0.14 (-0.27 to 0.001; P = .05), visuospatial -0.04 (-0.16 to 0.08; P = .53), motor -0.02 (-0.22 to 0.18; P = .83). Domains differ overall (chi-square(9) 41.14, P < .001) but learning, delayed memory, attention, speed and EF domains do not differ from each other after Bonferroni correction.

anchors.locator: Results › Preliminary Analyses, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Methods › Effect Size Calculation, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Funnel plot asymmetric; Egger test t = 4.70, P < .001. Duval-Tweedie trim-and-fill (random-effects, as no method exists for the multivariate model) added 44 effect sizes and reduced d by about 37.9%, from -0.206 (-0.24 to -0.16) to -0.128 (-0.17 to -0.09), still P < .001; authors advise caution about the exact reduction.

No difference by sample age category, early vs late onset, alcohol matching or publication period; mean age, age at first use and depression difference not associated. Treatment-seeking samples k = 12, n = 581, d -0.43 (-0.62 to -0.24) vs non-treatment-seeking k = 56, n = 8146, d -0.22 (-0.29 to -0.14); chi-square(1) 4.32, uncorrected P = .04.

Required abstinence >72 h: k = 15, n = 928, d -0.08 (-0.22 to 0.07), P = .29; smaller than <=72 h (k = 54, n = 7799), chi-square(1) 6.36, P = .01; mean reported abstinence (k = 28) beta 0.059, P = .04 at an uncorrected threshold. The -0.30 (-0.37 to -0.22) value for the 54 studies is printed in the Abstract.

anchors.locator: Methods › Effect Size Calculation, 1st paragraph; Methods › Study Eligibility, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Standardized mean difference d with Hedges-Olkin small-sample correction, inverse-variance weighted; negative d = worse performance in the cannabis group. Inclusion: mean age 26 or younger; heavy, frequent and/or problematic use as primary variable; not acute effects; comparison group; at least one standardized neurocognitive test; English; cross-sectional only.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 3rd, 4th and 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Samples mostly frequent users or people with cannabis use disorder, so findings may not apply to occasional use or medical cannabinoids; effects may be overestimates (small-study effects); analyses primarily used raw scores and do not account for sociodemographic, psychiatric or substance use confounders; no causal conclusion because pre-use deficits are not accounted for.

key_findings.note: Confirmed against the text and against Figure 1 (viewed 2026-10-31): 2,562 database records plus 30 from other searching; 1,324 after duplicates, all reviewed by title and abstract; 961 excluded as unrelated; 363 full texts assessed; 74 met inclusion criteria; 5 had overlapping samples; 69 studies included.

Figure 1 viewed 2026-10-31: the 13 reasons and their counts are as listed (67, 48, 35, 34, 29, 19, 17, 16, 8, 7, 5, 3, 1). They sum to 289 against the printed box total of 291. Exclusion of longitudinal follow-ups confirmed in Methods › Study Eligibility, 2nd paragraph.
All values as printed; this reader's own parse of the Table gives the same 62 publications, column sums 2,188 and 6,573, and the Philadelphia cohort's share (3,401 of 6,575 = 51.7%).
Prediction interval recomputed: -0.247 +/- 1.96 x sqrt(0.070 + 0.038^2) = -0.771 to +0.277 (same).

key_findings.correction: The finding's numbers are all correct, but its note is wrong: the more-than-72-hours interval (-0.22 to 0.07) does NOT include the overall estimate (-0.247); it overlaps the overall interval (-0.32 to -0.17) only between -0.22 and -0.17. Suggested note: 'A between-study comparison, not a within-person change. The more-than-72-hours interval includes no difference and reaches -0.22, close to the overall -0.25, so it does not exclude a deficit of nearly the overall size. The -0.30 estimate for the other 54 studies is printed only in the Abstract. The authors describe the abstinence associations as holding at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons (Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph).' The same error is in interpretation_gap (point 2) and analysis.power, and was carried into claim cl_can_cognition_after_stopping.

key_findings.note: Reproduced independently in step 1: the same 15 rows (168 to 2,160 h), the same 7 Tapert references (11, 54, 55, 61, 67, 78, 90) plus ref 62, 11 age ranges ending at 20 or younger, and 947 against 928.
The same paragraph also says the abstinence associations hold only at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons; worth adding to this finding.

reporting_issues.note: 384 / 69 = 5.57; a mean of 9.46 per study would imply about 653 effect sizes.
Figure 1 viewed 2026-10-31: the box reads 291; the reasons sum to 289; 363 - 289 = 74, the number meeting criteria.

All seven two-row publications and the identical Tait rows verified. The consequence that totals count shared comparison groups twice fits the numbers: the Table's comparison column sums to 6,573 against the reported 6,575, while counting each shared group once would give about 616 fewer (26 + 49 + 16 + 59 + 28 + 18 + 420).
Same sums in this reader's parse: 2,188; 6,573; 8,761; 947; 7,814.

Methods › Data Extraction cites eTable 1 for tests by domain; the Table footnote and Limitations cite eTable 2 for the per-study overview and use measures; the Supplementary Materials list names them the other way round.
Introduction, 4th paragraph and Discussion › Length of Abstinence, 1st paragraph, as stated.

The univariate random-effects basis is stated (Methods › Effect Size Calculation, 2nd paragraph). That the 384 effect sizes were treated as independent, and that the Egger test was done the same way, is the editors' inference from the narrower interval; the article does not say. Keep it labelled as an inference.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low under AMSTAR 2. Items 2, 7 and 9 fail on their own, so the overall rating holds even if item 4 (decided under senior decision 21) or item 11 (a close call, as the card says) were judged otherwise. Item 13 'yes' is generous, since no study was appraised and the Abstract and Key Points state the abstinence conclusion without caveats, but the Discussion does discuss confounding, pre-existing deficits and small-study bias, which meets the item's wording for non-randomized studies. Provisional, because the supplement was not read.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right: the Abstract, Key Points and Conclusions speak of deficits being diminished or restored with abstinence, but the evidence is a between-study, uncorrected moderator result. One correction to point (2): the more-than-72-hours interval (-0.22 to 0.07) does not include the overall estimate (-0.247). The conclusion that the result does not show that no deficit remains still holds, because the interval reaches -0.22, close to the overall value.

missed: analysis.power repeats the interval error ('whose interval (-0.22 to 0.07) includes the overall estimate'): it does not, since -0.247 lies below -0.22. Correct it together with key finding 7 and interpretation_gap point 2; claim cl_can_cognition_after_stopping carries the same wrong clause.

The authors themselves say the abstinence associations hold only at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons (Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph). The card says the P = .01 test is one of several moderator analyses, but no key finding records the authors' own statement. Claims that cite P = .01 should mark it as uncorrected.

Discussion, 1st paragraph (before the first subheading): the authors cite the National Academies report (ref. 91) as concluding there is significant uncertainty about cannabis-associated cognitive deficits after sustained abstinence. It appears only in the replication timeline; as a key finding it would support the 'insufficient evidence, disputed' framing of cl_can_cognition_after_stopping (minor).
